new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked every saved Open Library search-inside file under Each clause of the quoted p. 30 passage is present as scanned text from the three Turner facsimile scans (bwb_P8-ADR-779, americannegrohis0000unse_e1b4, africanismsingul0000turn; Arno 1969, xi+317 pp., access-restricted): "The accentuation of Gullah words of more than one syllable is indicated by the mark (') placed before", "before the syllable for the main stress and placed before the syllable for the secondary stress, when", "secondary stress, when it is thought necessary to indicate the secondary stress. Wholly unstressed syllables are unmarked. The accentuation and intonation of Gullah words vary somewhat with individual speaker…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Turner gives no positional rule: main stress is a property of each polysyllabic word and is marked word by word in his lists (as for its English lexifier), speakers vary in accentuation, and pitch/tone on words is not phonemic (only sentence-level intonation patterns and some non-English tone contours on words such as [ba,kra,] 'white man'). Best provisional reading: lexical (English-type, unpredictable) word stress, non-tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress exists and is marked with 'when it is thought necessary'; no rule for its placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Accentuation 'vary[ies] somewhat with individual speakers'; some words and short phrases carry 'non-English tones' (level, falling, rising contours), e.g. ba,kra 'white man', haz,ban 'husband'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level notation for the lexical items (chiefly African-derived personal names and words) in Turner's ch. 3 lists; the tone/intonation statements concern sentence-level patterns and tone contours on words and short phrases. Speech of basilectal Sea Island speakers recorded 1932-1940s (SC and GA coast).
new_statements.identity_note: Turner 1949 describes basilectal Gullah of the South Carolina and Georgia Sea Islands (fieldwork 1932-1940s), the same variety as gull1241 (Sea Island Creole English, ISO gul); Weldon and Klein also treat this variety. No dialect split is at issue. Afro-Seminole Creole (afro1254) is a separate Glottolog language and not covered.
